title: Cowardice the mother of cruelty
paragraphs: I have often heard it said that cowardice is the mother of cruelty, and I have found by experience that malicious, inhuman animosity and ferocity usually go hand in hand with a kind of feminine weakness. I have seen the most cruel people apt to cry on trivial occasions. Alexander, the tyrant of Pherae, did not dare watch tragedies in the theatre, for fear his citizens should see him weep at the misfortunes of Hecuba and Andromache — the same man who without pity had so many people murdered every day. Is it not meanness of spirit that makes them so pliable to every extreme? Valour, whose effect is to be exercised only against resistance —
"Nec nisi bellantis gaudet cervice juvenci" —
["Nor delights in killing a bull unless he resists." — Claudius, Ep. ad Hadrianum, v. 39.]

stops when it sees the enemy at its mercy. But pusillanimity, to claim that it too was in the game, not having dared to take part in the first act of danger, takes for itself the second act, of blood and massacre. The murders in victories are usually carried out by the riff-raff and camp-followers of an army; and what causes so many unheard-of cruelties in domestic wars is that this rabble makes war by plunging itself up to the elbows in blood and ripping open a body that lies prostrate at its feet, having no sense of any other kind of valour:
"Et lupus, et turpes instant morientibus ursi, Et quaecunque minor nobilitate fera est:"
["Wolves and the filthy bears, and all the baser beasts, fall upon the dying." — Ovid, Trist., iii. 5, 35.]

Like cowardly dogs that at home worry and tear the skins of wild beasts they dared not come near in the field. What is it in our times that makes our quarrels deadly, so that, where our fathers had several degrees of revenge, we now begin with the last, and at the first meeting nothing is to be said but "kill"? What is this but cowardice?

Everyone can see that there is more bravery and disdain in subduing an enemy than in cutting his throat, in making him yield than in putting him to the sword; besides which, the appetite for revenge is more satisfied and pleased when its only aim is to make itself felt. That is why we do not fall on a beast or a stone when they hurt us, because they are incapable of being aware of our revenge; and to kill a man is to save him from the injury and offence we mean to do him. As Bias cried out to a wicked fellow, "I know that sooner or later you will have your reward, but I am afraid I will not be there to see it"; and pitied the Orchomenians because the penitence of Lyciscus for the treason committed against them came at a time when no one remained alive of those who had been hurt by the offence and whom the pleasure of this penitence might have reached. Revenge is to be pitied when the person on whom it is exercised is robbed of any means of suffering under it; for, as the avenger means to look on and enjoy the pleasure of his revenge, so the person he takes revenge on must be a spectator too, in order to be afflicted and to repent. "He will be sorry for it," we say — and because we have given him a pistol shot through the head, do we imagine he will be sorry? On the contrary, if we look closely, we will see that he pulls a face at us as he falls, and is so far from regret that he does not even reproach us; and we do him the kindest service in life, which is to make him die without feeling it, and quickly. We then have to hide and dodge the officers of justice who hunt us, while he is at rest. Killing is good for preventing an offence to come, not for avenging one that is already past, and is more an act of fear than of bravery, of precaution than of courage, of defence than of attack. It is plain that by killing we lose both the true end of revenge and the care of our reputation; we are afraid that, if he lives, he will do us another injury as great as the first. It is not out of animosity toward him but out of concern for yourself that you get rid of him.

In the kingdom of Narsinga this remedy would be useless to us, where not only soldiers but tradesmen as well end their disputes by the sword. The king never refuses a field to any who want to fight, and if they are persons of quality he looks on himself, rewarding the victor with a chain of gold — for which anyone who pleases may fight with him again, so that, having survived one combat, the victor has signed up for many.

If by means of our courage we thought we could always be masters of our enemies and triumph over them at our pleasure, we would be sorry to see them escape us as they do, by dying. But we want victory more for safety than for honour, and in our quarrels we pursue the result more than the glory.

Asinius Pollio, who, as being a worthy man, was the less to be excused, committed a similar fault when, having written a libel against Plancus, he held it back until Plancus was dead — which is to bite your thumb at a blind man, to insult a deaf one, to wound a man who feels nothing, rather than to risk his retort. And it was also said of him that only goblins wrestle with the dead.

Anyone who waits for the author to die whose writings he intends to challenge — what does he say of himself but that he is weak in attack? It was told to Aristotle that someone had spoken ill of him. "Let him do more," he said; "let him whip me too, provided I am not there."

Our fathers were content to answer an insult with the lie, the lie with a box on the ear, and so on. They were brave enough not to fear their adversaries, alive and provoked; we tremble with fear at the very sight of them on their feet. And the truth of this — does it not show in our admirable practice these days, of going after to the death both the man who has offended us and the man we have offended? It is also a kind of cowardice that has introduced the custom of having seconds, thirds, and fourths in our duels. They used to be duels — now they are skirmishes, scuffles, and battles. Solitude must have been terrifying to those who first invented this practice:
"Quum in se cuique minimum fiduciae esset,"

for in danger any kind of company is naturally consoling. Originally, third persons were called in only to prevent disorder and foul play, and to be witnesses to the outcome of the combat; but now things have gone so far that the witnesses themselves join in. Whoever is invited cannot decently stand by as an idle spectator, on pain of being suspected either of want of affection or of want of courage. Quite apart from the injustice and unworthiness of such a thing — of bringing in another man's strength and valour to defend your honour — I see it as a disadvantage to a brave man who relies on himself alone, to mix his fortune with that of a second. Every man runs danger enough on his own account without taking on the risks of someone else, and has enough to do to trust to his own valour for the defence of his life, without putting something so precious into a third man's hands. For unless it has been expressly agreed in advance to the contrary, it becomes a four-way combat, and if your second is killed, you have two on your hands, with good reason; and as for calling it foul play, it is so, yes — as it is foul play, when fully armed, to attack a man who has only the hilt of a broken sword in his hand, or, while clear and untouched, to attack one who is grievously wounded; but if these are advantages you have gained in the course of fighting, you may use them without reproach. The disparity and inequality are weighed and reckoned only from the condition of the combatants at the start; as for the rest, you must take your chance. Even if alone you had three enemies on you at once, your two companions being killed, you have no more wrong done to you than I would do in a battle by running through a man I saw engaged with one of our own, in just the same kind of advantage. The nature of group fighting is such that, where there is troop against troop — as when our Duke of Orleans challenged Henry, king of England, a hundred against a hundred; three hundred against as many, as the Argives against the Lacedaemonians; three against three, as the Horatii against the Curiatii — the multitude on each side is treated as one single man; the risk is mingled and mixed whenever there is company.

I have a domestic interest in this discussion, for my brother, the Sieur de Matecoulom, was at Rome asked by a gentleman he hardly knew, and who was the defendant challenged by another, to be his second; in this duel he found himself paired with a gentleman much better known to him. (I would dearly like an explanation of these rules of honour that so often crash against, and confound, those of reason.) Having dispatched his man and seeing the two principals still on their feet and unhurt, he ran in to disengage his friend. What less could he have done? Should he have stood still, and, if luck had so ordered it, watched the man he had come to defend killed in front of him? What he had done so far did not help the case; the quarrel was still undecided. The courtesy that you can and certainly ought to show your enemy, when you have brought him to a bad pass and have a great advantage over him, I do not see how you can show it when another man's interest is involved, when you are only there as an assistant and the quarrel is not yours; he could be neither just nor courteous at the cost of the man he was there to serve. For this he was released from the prisons of Italy at the prompt and solemn request of our king. Indiscreet nation! We are not satisfied with letting the world know our vices and follies by report alone; we must go to foreign countries to show in person what fools we are. Put three Frenchmen in the deserts of Libya, and they will not live a month together without fighting; so that you would think this travel was deliberately designed to give foreigners the pleasure of our tragedies — and, for the most part, to such as rejoice and laugh at our miseries. We go to Italy to learn fencing, and practise the art at the cost of our lives before we have learned it; though by the rule of discipline we should put theory before practice. We give ourselves away as beginners:
"Primitae juvenum miserae, bellique futuri Dura rudimenta."
["Wretched the elementary trials of youth, and hard the rudiments of approaching war." — Virgil, Aeneid, xi. 156.]

I know that fencing is an art very useful to its end (in a duel between two princes, cousins-german, in Spain, the elder, says Livy, by his skill and dexterity in arms easily overcame the greater and clumsier strength of the younger), and one whose knowledge, as I know from experience, has given some men courage beyond their natural measure. But this is not properly valour, because it leans on technique and rests on something other than itself. The honour of combat consists in the rivalry of courage, not of skill; and this is why I have known a friend of mine, famous as a great master in this art, in his quarrels choose such weapons as would strip him of the advantage, weapons that depended wholly on luck and steadiness, so that his victory would not be put down more to his skill in fencing than to his valour. When I was young, gentlemen avoided the reputation of being good fencers as something against them, and learned to fence with all possible secrecy, as a craft of cunning that detracted from true and natural valour:

"Non schivar non parar, non ritirarsi, Voglion costor, ne qui destrezza ha parte; Non danno i colpi or finti, or pieni, or scarsi! Toglie l'ira a il furor l'uso de l'arte. Odi le spade orribilmente utarsi A mezzo il ferro; il pie d'orma non parte, Sempre a il pie fermo, a la man sempre in moto; Ne scende taglio in van, ne punta a voto."

["They neither shrank, nor vantage sought of ground, They travers'd not, nor skipt from part to part, Their blows were neither false, nor feigned found: In fight, their rage would let them use no art. Their swords together clash with dreadful sound, Their feet stand fast, and neither stir nor start, They move their hands, steadfast their feet remain. Nor blow nor foin they strook, or thrust in vain." — Tasso, Gierus. Lib., c. 12, st. 55, Fairfax's translation.]

Archery contests, tilting, and barriers — mock versions of warlike fighting — were the exercises of our forefathers. This other exercise is less noble in proportion as it serves only a private end; it teaches us to destroy one another against law and justice, and it always produces very bad effects. It is far more worthy and becoming to train ourselves in things that strengthen rather than weaken our state, things that aim at public safety and common glory. The consul Publius Rutilius was the first to teach his soldiers to handle their arms with skill and to join art with valour — not for the purposes of private quarrel, but for war and the contests of the people of Rome, a popular and civic defence. And besides the example of Caesar, who ordered his men to aim chiefly at the faces of Pompey's soldiers in the battle of Pharsalia, a thousand other commanders have thought to invent new forms of weapons and new ways of striking and defending, as the occasion required.

But just as Philopoemen condemned wrestling, in which he excelled, because the preparations involved in it differed from those that belong to military discipline, to which alone he held that men of honour should give themselves wholly, so it seems to me that this technique to which we accustom our limbs, these twists and motions young men are taught in this new school, are not only useless but actually contrary and harmful to the practice of fighting in battle. Our people also commonly use particular weapons specially designed for the duel, and I have seen it disapproved when a gentleman challenged to fight with rapier and dagger turned up in the equipment of a man-at-arms, or when another took his cloak instead of his dagger. It is worth noting that Laches in Plato, speaking of learning to fence in our manner, says he never knew any great soldier come out of that school, especially among the masters; and indeed, as for them, our own experience says the same. As for the rest, we may at least conclude that they are qualities with no relation or correspondence to each other; and in the education of the children of his republic, Plato bans the art of boxing, introduced by Amycus and Epeius, and that of wrestling, by Antaeus and Cercyon, because they have another end than fitting young men for the service of war, and contribute nothing to it. But I see I have somewhat wandered from my theme.

The Emperor Mauricius, warned by dreams and various omens that a certain Phocas, an obscure soldier, would kill him, asked his son-in-law Philip who this Phocas was, what his nature, qualities, and manners were like; and as soon as Philip, among other things, told him the man was cowardly and timid, the emperor immediately concluded that he was a murderer and cruel. What is it that makes tyrants so bloody? Only the anxiety for their own safety, and that their faint hearts can find them no other means of securing themselves than by wiping out those who might hurt them, even down to women, for fear of a scratch:
"Cuncta ferit, dum cuncta timer."
["He strikes at all who fears all." — Claudius, in Eutrop., i. 182.]

The first cruelties are committed for their own sake; from these springs the fear of a just revenge, which afterwards produces a series of new cruelties, to wipe one another out. Philip, king of Macedon, who had so much to do with the Roman people, harrowed by the horror of so many murders committed by his order, and doubting whether he could keep himself safe from so many families he had mortally injured and offended over the years, resolved to seize all the children of those he had had killed and to dispatch them one after another, day by day, and so secure his own repose.

Fine matter is never out of place wherever you put it, and so I, who care more about the weight and usefulness of what I say than about its order and connection, need not be afraid here to bring in an excellent story, even if it is somewhat off to the side; for when they have their own native beauty and can stand on their own merits, the least pretext will serve to draw them into my discourse.

Among others condemned by Philip had been one Herodicus, prince of Thessaly; after him, Philip had had both his sons-in-law put to death, each leaving a young son behind. Theoxena and Archo were their two widows. Theoxena, though much courted to do so, could not be persuaded to remarry. Archo married Poris, the leading man among the Aenians, and had a great many children by him, whom, when she died, she left at a very tender age. Theoxena, moved by maternal affection for her nephews so as to have them under her own eyes and in her own care, married Poris. Then suddenly came the king's edict. This brave-spirited mother, suspecting Philip's cruelty and afraid of what the soldiers would do to these charming and tender children, was bold enough to declare that she would rather kill them with her own hands than hand them over. Poris, startled by this protest, promised to spirit them away and take them to Athens, to put them in the care of some faithful friends of his. They took advantage of an annual festival held at Aenia in honour of Aeneas, and went there. After appearing by day at the public ceremonies and the banquet, they slipped at night into a vessel set ready for the purpose, to escape by sea. The wind was contrary, and finding themselves in the morning in sight of the land they had left overnight, and being pursued by the port guards, Poris saw what was happening and did all he could to make the sailors strain to outrun the pursuers. But Theoxena, frantic with love and revenge, in keeping with her earlier resolution, prepared weapons and poison and laid them out in front of the children. "Come, my children," she said, "death is now the only means of your defence and freedom, and shall give the gods an opportunity to exercise their holy justice. These sharp swords and these full cups will open you the way to it; take courage, fear nothing. And you, my son, who are the eldest, take this steel in your hand, that you may die the more bravely." The children, with so powerful a counsellor on one side and the enemy at their throats on the other, all snatched eagerly at whatever was nearest to hand and, half dead, were thrown into the sea. Theoxena, proud of having so gloriously provided for the safety of her children, clasped her arms with great affection round her husband's neck. "Let us, my friend," she said, "follow these boys, and share the same tomb." And so, embraced, they threw themselves headlong into the sea, so that the ship was carried back without its owners into the harbour.

Tyrants, in order at once to kill and to make their anger felt, have used their ingenuity to invent the most lingering deaths. They want their enemies dispatched — but not so fast that they will not have time to taste their vengeance. And on this score they are sorely perplexed; for if the torments they inflict are intense, they are short; if long, they are not as painful as they wish; and so they torment themselves over the choice of the greatest cruelty. We have a thousand examples of this in antiquity, and I am not sure that we do not, unawares, retain some traces of that barbarity.

Anything that goes beyond a simple death appears to me sheer cruelty. Our justice cannot expect that the man who is not restrained by the fear of being beheaded or hanged should be any more awed by the imagination of a slow fire, pincers, or the wheel. And meanwhile I do not know whether we are not driving them to despair, for what can be the state of a man's soul as he waits twenty-four hours together to be broken on a wheel, or, in the old way, nailed to a cross? Josephus relates that in the time of the war the Romans waged in Judaea, happening to pass a place where they had crucified some Jews three days before, he recognised three of his friends among them, and obtained the favour of having them taken down; two of them, he says, died, but the third lived a long time afterwards.

Chalcondylas, a writer of good credit, in the records he has left of things that happened in his own time and near at hand, tells us, as the most excessive of torments, of one the Emperor Mohammed often practised: cutting men in two across the diaphragm with a single stroke of a scimitar, so that they died two deaths at once. Both parts, he says, were seen to twitch and struggle for a long time after, in very great torment. I do not think there was much suffering in that movement: the torments that look most dreadful are not always the worst to endure, and I find that those other historians report of him to have been done to the Epirot lords are more horrible and cruel, where they were sentenced to be flayed alive piecemeal, in such a malicious way that they remained fifteen days in that misery.

And these other two: Croesus, having seized a gentleman who was a favourite of his brother Pantaleon, carried him into a fuller's shop, where he had him scratched and combed with the cards and combs of that trade until he died. George Sechel, chief commander of the peasants of Poland, who committed so many atrocities under the name of the Crusade, after being defeated in battle and captured by the Voivode of Transylvania, was bound naked on a rack for three days, exposed to every torment that anyone could devise against him; during which time many other prisoners were kept fasting; in the end, while he was still alive and looking on, they made his beloved brother Lucat, for whom alone he had pleaded, taking all the blame of their crimes upon himself, drink his blood; and they made twenty of his most favoured captains feed on him, tearing his flesh in pieces with their teeth and swallowing the morsels. The rest of his body and his bowels, as soon as he was dead, were boiled, and others of his followers were forced to eat them.
